hints: Focus on the word uncontrolled. A tumour means cells are cycling much faster than normal, so ask yourself which part of the cycle normally takes up most of the time.
Remember that interphase (G1, S and G2 with growth and checkpoints) is about 90% of a normal cycle, while mitosis itself is already quick and cannot get much shorter.
walkthrough:
**What a tumour tells us**

Think of a tumour as cells in a hurry. They divide again and again with very short gaps in between.

So the total cell cycle time must get shorter.

**Recall normal timing of the cycle**

In a normal cell, interphase is by far the longest stage. The cell grows, copies its DNA in S phase, and pauses at checkpoints in G1 and G2.

Mitosis plus cytokinesis is relatively short, it just divides what has already been prepared.

**Decide what gets shortened**

To divide faster, cancer cells rush through growth and skip or ignore the checkpoints in interphase. Mitosis still has to separate chromosomes carefully, so its time changes very little.

Therefore interphase is the part that takes much less time.

options.A: Cytokinesis is already very brief and just splits the cytoplasm, it is not the main time-saving step in rapid division.
options.B: Interphase is normally the longest phase with growth and checkpoints. In tumour cells checkpoints are bypassed, so G1 and G2 are greatly shortened.
options.C: Mitosis is already short and must still accurately separate chromatids, so tumour cells do not greatly shorten it.
options.D: Telophase is only one small part of mitosis, so shortening it alone could not explain the much faster overall cycle.
